title: Eigenvalue-versus-time (symlog): how stiff is it along the trajectory?
summary: How stiff is the problem right now? The real part of the fastest eigenvalue is plotted against time on a symmetric-log axis, so very large negative values and values near zero can sit on one scale. Two curves compare coordinate systems.

media.alt: Plot of Re(lambda) against log time with a symmetric-log y axis: the original-coordinates curve rises from about -1e5 to about -50 by 4 ms; the transformed curve rises from about -320 to about -20.
media.caption: Reference render of class F6.1 (design-system gallery). The data are synthetic and exist only to demonstrate the form.

source.note: Plot class from the design system's plot taxonomy; synthetic demonstration data.

read_the_figure.question: How stiff is it along the trajectory?
read_the_figure.axes: x: time in seconds, logarithmic (1e-6 to 1). y: Re(lambda) in 1/s on a symmetric logarithmic axis with linear threshold 10 (linear inside plus or minus 10, logarithmic outside).
look_at: How large is |Re(lambda)| at the start, and how long does it take to fall to its late value?
How far apart are the two curves at early time, and at late time?
Does any curve enter the linear band (plus or minus 10) or cross zero (a change of stability)?
Is the symlog threshold stated, and does the picture say which eigenvalue is plotted?
as_drawn: Original coordinates (teal solid): Re(lambda) starts at about -1e5 and settles at about -50 once the fast mode has died near 3 to 4 ms.
Transformed coordinates (amber dashed): about -320 at the start and about -20 at late time.
At t = 1e-6 s the curves differ by a factor of about 310, at t = 1 s by 2.5.
The axis label says symlog with threshold 10, but the figure does not say which eigenvalue is plotted; it is assumed to be the stiffest one.
read_the_figure.proves: The curves show how the fastest time scale of the linearised problem evolves, and so when an explicit method is restricted. They do not show the whole spectrum, only one eigenvalue per curve, and are silent on accuracy.
if_wrong: A curve that crosses zero: the linearisation changes stability there; a symlog axis shows this but a log axis could not.
No stated threshold: the reader cannot tell where the axis switches from linear to logarithmic and may misread distances.
Curves that are plotted at different times or from different trajectories: the comparison is not like for like.
must_check: symlog threshold stated: the axis is linear inside the threshold and logarithmic outside, so the reader needs the threshold to read any distance on the plot.

terms.meaning: A number describing how a small perturbation grows or decays along the solution: it is exp(lambda t) in the linearised problem.
A problem is stiff when its eigenvalues have very different magnitudes and the stable step is set by the largest, not by the accuracy needed.
A logarithmic axis made usable around zero by being linear inside a threshold: it can show values of either sign and zero.
A component of the solution that decays on a very short time scale, 1 / |lambda|.
The largest step an explicit method can take, c / |lambda|max, with c about 2.785 for RK4.

remember: Re(lambda) < 0 means decay; the time scale is 1 / |Re(lambda)|.
A symlog axis is linear inside plus or minus its threshold, so always read the threshold.
Compare curves at the same times and on the same trajectory.
Falling |lambda| during a run means the stiffness is transient.

understand.title: Marks and encodings
understand.text: Position on x is time on a log scale; position on y is the real part of the stiffest eigenvalue on a symmetric-log scale. Two line styles and colours separate the original and the transformed coordinates. The tick labels read 10^3, 10^2, 10^1, 0, then the negative decades, so both signs share one axis.

understand.title: Why this form answers the question
understand.text: Plain language: the more negative the eigenvalue, the faster something dies and the smaller the explicit step must be. Plotting it against time shows when the problem is hardest (early, here) and when it relaxes. The symlog axis is needed because the values span five decades and may change sign; a plain log axis cannot draw a negative number.

understand.title: How it misleads
understand.text: Symlog distorts distances: the stretch between 0 and plus or minus 10 is linear while the rest is logarithmic, so apparent slopes change at the threshold. One eigenvalue is not the spectrum; the smallest eigenvalue and the gap between them also matter. A curve that looks flat at late time may still have a big ratio between its fastest and slowest mode. Eigenvalues of a nonnormal Jacobian also under-describe transient growth.

understand.title: Alternatives
understand.text: A plot of the stiffness ratio |lambda|max / |lambda|min against time is a single curve and avoids the symlog axis. A before and after bar chart of the whole spectrum (F6.2) shows compression. The step-size trace with its ceiling (F5.4) shows the consequence for the solver.

understand.title: A variant to create
understand.text: Plot both the largest and the smallest eigenvalue magnitude for each coordinate system, shade the linear band of the symlog axis, and add the RK4 stable step on a second y axis on the right.

steps.title: Decay time and explicit step limit
steps.note: The perturbation decays with time scale tau; the explicit step must stay below c divided by the largest |lambda|.

steps.title: A fast mode that dies out
steps.note: Time until the transient part is a given amount epsilon above its late value. In the render a = 1e5 and tau = 1/3000 s.

steps.title: The ratio between curves
steps.note: The relative step you could take in the transformed coordinates if stability were the only limit.

worked.title: Reading the stiffness history from the reference render
worked.problem: (1) What are the original and transformed values of Re(lambda) at t = 1e-6 s? (2) What explicit RK4 step does each allow at that time? (3) When has the fast mode in the original coordinates died to within 1 percent of the late value?

solution.text: (1) Reading the curves at the left edge: about -1e5 for the original and about -3.2e2 for the transformed.
(2) Divide RK4's real-axis limit by the magnitude.
The transformed system allows a step about 310 times larger.
(3) The late value is -50, so 1 percent is 0.5. Solve the decay for the transient part to equal 0.5.

worked.answer: About -1e5 and -320; explicit steps of 2.8e-5 s and 8.7e-3 s (a ratio of about 310); the fast mode is gone to within one percent by about 4 ms.

analyze.q: Why does the gap between the curves close at late time and what does that mean for the benefit of the transformation?
analyze.hint: Compare the values at t = 1 s.

analyze.q: Neither curve enters the band between -10 and 10. What would it mean if one did?
analyze.hint: Sign changes and the linear region.

analyze.q: Why is it not enough to plot only the largest eigenvalue?
analyze.hint: What defines stiffness: an absolute size or a ratio?

evaluate.q: A method is chosen because the transformed curve is 300 times smaller at early time. Is that enough to expect a 300-fold speedup?
evaluate.hint: Late-time behaviour, cost per step, and accuracy.

create: Redraw the plot with a plain log axis of |Re(lambda)| and compare the readability with the symlog version.
Add the smallest eigenvalue to each curve and print the stiffness ratio at t = 1e-6 and t = 1.

checks.q: Why use a symmetric log axis here and not a plain log axis?
checks.hint: What values must the axis hold?
checks.answer: The eigenvalue is negative (and could change sign), and a plain log axis cannot show negative values or zero; symlog is linear near zero and logarithmic outside.

checks.q: Re(lambda) = -2000 per second. What is the RK4 stable step?
The original curve is flat at -50 for t > 4 ms. Is the problem still stiff?
checks.hint: Think about the ratio of the largest to the smallest magnitude.
checks.answer: Not because of this eigenvalue alone: stiffness is a ratio of time scales. If a slower mode of, say, 0.1 per second is present, the ratio 500 is still large and an explicit method is still step-limited by the 50 per second mode.
